ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: All experiments reported here were approved by the UNLV IRB.
Ethics approval: UNLV IRB, PROTOCOL TITLE: 710894-8 Encoding and Retrieval Processes, Consent to participate: All participants consented to take part in these experiments.
Participants were 30 University of Nevada, Las Vegas (UNLV) students (M age = 21.0, 22 women) recruited from the Psychology Department's subject pool who participated in return for course credit.
Participants were instructed to memorize each item as best they could for a later memory test, and they were told that trying to identify (or label) each item would help them to remember it.

Instructions for the recognition test followed each study task; participants were asked to use a 6-point response scale to make old/new decisions about each item, with 1 anchored as "Sure New" and 6 anchored as "Sure Old".
Participants were strongly encouraged to use the whole scale across the course of each test.

At test, sounds were played for the full 2s before participants were able to respond and pictures were displayed for the full 700ms before they could respond, matching the duration times during the study phase.
Sixty participants (Mage = 18.8, 41 women, 19 men) from the UNLV Psychology Department's subject pool took part in this experiment in return for course credit.

The task was a 2-back task, presented in the modality opposite of the stimuli being encoded; thus, the n-back task was presented in black font in the middle of the computer screen when participants were studying auditory items, and was presented over headphones when studying the visual objects.
Between the presentation of each target stimulus, a number was presented and participants had to decide whether it was the same as two numbers back or not.
Participants had three seconds to respond on n-back trials (via keyboard presses) in both the auditory and visual study phases, and they practiced the task before starting the first study phase.
Participants were told it was very important to perform well on the n-back task, and that they should also memorize the objects for a later memory test.
Participants were randomly assigned to either the full or divided attention condition, and modality remained a within-subjects variable.
Seventy-eight participants (M age = 19.4, 52 women, 26 men) from the UNLV Psychology Department's subject pool took part in this experiment in return for course credit.

Several additional participants completed the experiment, but their data were excluded from analyses (using preregistered criteria): three for not using enough of the confidence scale to form an ROC, five for not doing the DA task, three for failing to use the response scale correctly, and five for low performance (d a < .20).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: We used the recollection effect size from Experiment 2 to conduct a power analysis, which indicated a sample of 78, with 26 participants in each condition. Seventy-eight participants (M age = 19.4, 52 women, 26 men) from the UNLV Psychology Department's subject pool took part in this experiment in return for course credit. Several additional participants completed the experiment, but their data were excluded from analyses (using preregistered criteria): three for not using enough of the confidence scale to form an ROC, five for not doing the DA task, three for failing to use the response scale correctly, and five for low performance (d a < .20).

A power analysis based on the effect size in Experiment 3 was conducted and indicated a sample of 64 (32 participants in each attention condition). Sixty-four participants (M age = 20.0, 49 women) from the UNLV Psychology Department's subject pool participated in this experiment in return for course credit. Five additional participants took part in the study but their data were excluded from analyses because they failed to understand how to use the response scale (n = 2), had poor performance (d a < .20, n = 2), or did not complete the divided attention task (n = 1).

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Auditory and Visual Object Recognition
table.authors: Colleen M. Parks, Laura Werner, Joel S. Snyder, Margaret A. McMullin
table.description:
Memory for visual objects has been shown to be much better than memory for auditory objects. These differences have not yet been examined within the context of recognition memory models. 
In a previous study we used the dual process signal detection (DPSD) model and found that the recollection of visual and auditory objects differed more than the familiarity for those objects. In a second experiment, we found that dividing attention negatively affected recollection and familiarity, but did so to different degrees for the two modalities. Divided attention substantially reduced recollection of visual objects but not of auditory objects. Divided attention also reduced familiarity for visual objects, but less for auditory objects; this effect was substantially smaller than that found for recollection though. The full attention condition replicated the first study. 
In the divided attention condition in the previous study, we divided attention with an n-back task that was in the opposite modality of the studied items (e.g., studied auditory items were paired with a visual n-back task). In order to verify that the larger effects on visual recollection were not due to differing n-back tasks in the two conditions, the registered study will replicate the divided attention study and add a condition in which attention is divided with an n-back task in the same modality as the studied items (e.g., studied auditory items will be paired with an auditory n-back task). The broader question is: why does memory differ for auditory and visual objects? The specific question in this experiment is: does divided attention affect visual and auditory object memory differently?
table.research_questions:
The predicted alternative hypothesis is that there is an interaction between modality (auditory and visual) and attention (full, divided-same modality, divided-different modality), but that there are no differences between the two n-back tasks in terms of their effects on the memory processes. This will be tested with a 2 (modality) X 3 (divided attention same modality n-back, divided attention different modality n-back, full attention) mixed Bayesian ANOVA with modality as the within subjects factor and attention as the between subjects factor. This ANOVA will be conducted on recollection and familiarity model parameters separately, because they are on different scales. 
Recollection (probability estimate from the DPSD model): We expect main effects of modality (better visual recollection) and attention (better recollection in the full attention condition), and an interaction between modality and attention, with greater effects of attention on visual than on auditory memory, and no differences between the different ways of dividing attention. Looking specifically at the full attention condition, as a replication of two previous studies, we expect that recollection will be worse for auditory objects than for visual objects, and that this effect will be bigger than that found for familiarity.
Familiarity (d’ estimate from the DPSD model): Attention should negatively affect the familiarity estimates with greater familiarity in the full attention condition, and there should be an interaction between modality and attention, with larger effects of modality in the full attention condition than in the divided attention conditions. The effect size of this interaction is expected to be smaller than the effect size for the recollection interaction. Looking specifically at the full attention condition, as a replication of two previous studies, we expect that familiarity will be worse for auditory objects than for visual objects, but that the effect size will be smaller than that found for recollection.
Observed d’ (overall recognition, not estimated from the model): We expect an interaction between modality and attention is expected, with a greater difference between modalities in the full attention condition than in the divided attention condition.
Correlations between modalities for each memory process (e.g., the correlation between recollection of auditory and of visual objects) will be examined. Based on the previous experiment, a significant correlation is expected for familiarity estimates and observed d’, but not for recollection estimates.
The accuracy of the two attention tasks is expected to be the same, whereas the RTs are expected to be greater when the task is auditory.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
This will be a mixed design.
Independent variables: attention (3 between subjects groups) and modality (2 conditions, within subject)
Dependent variables: process estimates of recollection, process estimates of familiarity (d’), and overall recognition d’. 
The order of the tests will be counterbalanced: visual first or auditory first.
table.randomization:
At the level of items presented as stimuli, they will be newly randomized for each subject (randomly assigned to old or new status).
Participants will be randomly assigned to experimental conditions.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures:
We will be recruiting subjects from psychology classes at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. Students are either required to earn research credit for their classes, or are offered extra credit for their participation in research. Thus, subjects are compensated with research credits toward their classes. Some students also simply volunteer to take part in research without compensation. Students sign up for studies on a computerized system (SONA) that provides a brief description of each study.
To be eligible, students must be: between the ages of 18 and 40, have no diagnosed memory impairments, be sober, and be fluent in English.
table.sample_size: Our sample size is n = 78 human subjects.
table.sample_size_rationale: A power analysis using MorePower 6.0 based on effect sizes of a previous study indicated that we need 78 participants in order to achieve 80% power to detect an interaction with an effect size of partial-eta squared = .117 (the smallest effect size that showed some positive evidence of an interaction in the previous study). This will result in 26 people per attention condition; broken down further, it will be 13 people per counterbalance condition across the three attention conditions.
table.manipulated_variables:
Modality (visual or auditory objects)
Attention (divided attention with a n-back task in the same modality as the stimuli studied; divided attention with an n-back task in a different modality; full attention)
table.measured_variables: Measured variables include: confidence ratings in old/new judgments that will be submitted to the DPSD model to obtain estimates of recollection and familiarity. Recollection and familiarity will be analyzed; confidence ratings will not be directly analyzed. Confidence ratings will also be used to measure overall recognition (collapsed across recollection and familiarity) as indicated by d’. Accuracy and reaction time will be measured for the divided attention tasks.
table.statistical_tests:
Bayesian ANOVAs will be used to assess evidence for main effects and interactions between the variables. Effect sizes from frequentist statistics will also be obtained. Pearson correlations will examine the relationship between memory estimates across modalities (e.g., auditory recollection and visual recollection). Interactions will be followed up by simple main effects and t-tests. 
The predicted alternative hypothesis is that there is an interaction between modality (auditory and visual) and attention (full, divided-same modality, divided-different modality), but that there are no differences between the two n-back tasks in terms of their effects on the memory processes. This will be tested with a 2 (modality) X 3 (divided attention same modality n-back, divided attention different modality n-back, full attention) mixed Bayesian ANOVA with modality as the within subjects factor and attention as the between subjects factor. This ANOVA will be conducted on recollection and familiarity model parameters separately, because they are on different scales. 
Recollection (probability estimate from the DPSD model): We expect main effects of modality (better visual recollection) and attention (better recollection in the full attention condition), and an interaction between modality and attention, with greater effects of attention on visual than on auditory memory, and no differences between the different ways of dividing attention. Looking specifically at the full attention condition, as a replication of two previous studies, we expect that recollection will be worse for auditory objects than for visual objects, and that this effect will be bigger than that found for familiarity.
Familiarity (d’ estimate from the DPSD model): Attention should negatively affect the familiarity estimates with greater familiarity in the full attention condition, and there should be an interaction between modality and attention, with larger effects of modality in the full attention condition than in the divided attention conditions. The effect size of this interaction is expected to be smaller than the effect size for the recollection interaction. Looking specifically at the full attention condition, as a replication of two previous studies, we expect that familiarity will be worse for auditory objects than for visual objects, but that the effect size will be smaller than that found for recollection.
Observed d’ (overall recognition, not estimated from the model): We expect an interaction between modality and attention is expected, with a greater difference between modalities in the full attention condition than in the divided attention condition.
Correlations between modalities for each memory process (e.g., the correlation between recollection of auditory and of visual objects) will be examined. Based on the previous experiment, a significant correlation is expected for familiarity estimates and observed d’, but not for recollection estimates.
Attention task (2) X modality mixed design ANOVAs will be used to examine potential differences in accuracy across conditions and differences in RTs across condition. For accuracy, we expect weak-to-no evidence for the interaction. For RTs, we expect greater RTs in the auditory n-back task than in the visual n-back task.
table.inference_criteria: We will use frequentist statistics to obtain partial-eta-squared for the interactions, but will use Bayesian analyses to make inferences. Cohen’s d will be calculated using means and standard deviations for t-tests. Bayes factors guidelines will be taken from Raftery (1995).
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Data will be excluded when the subject does not use enough of the 1 – 6 confidence scale to form a receiver operating characteristic, or when they flip or otherwise misunderstand how to use the response scale. Data that show floor level performance (overall recognition d’ < .20) will be excluded. Data points that are 2.5 or more standard deviations from the mean will be treated as outliers and will be excluded from the analyses (this will be based on memory measures, as well as accuracy and reaction times for the divided attention tests). Such cases will be replaced with new subjects in order to reach the necessary sample size.
Data will also be excluded if: 1) the subject is over 40 years old, 2) the subject is intoxicated, or 3) the subject has a diagnosed memory disorder (e.g., memory impairments due to epilepsy).
table.additional_comments: This experiment is a replication and extension of two previous (unregistered) experiments examining effects of modality and attention on measures of recollection and familiarity.

table.title: Auditory and Visual Object Recognition: Equating Modalities with Repetition
table.research_questions:
Hypotheses will be tested with a 2 (modality: audio 2x & visual 1x) X 2 (attention: divided attention & full attention) mixed Bayesian ANOVA with modality as the within-subjects factor, and attention as the between-subjects factor. This ANOVA will be conducted on recollection (probability estimate from the DPSD model), familiarity (d’ estimate from the DPSD model), and overall recognition (da, calculated from confidence ratings for hits and false alarms).

Possibility 1:
We may equate da (overall recognition) for the two modalities in the FA condition for auditory 2x and visual 1x, we may fail to do so, or we may attenuate the differences but fail to eliminate them. If we succeed, we expect the effects listed below will still be present but will be attenuated compared to previous studies (as indicated by effect sizes). If we attenuate the difference between modalities, but do not equate them, we expect to see the same patterns we’ve found before, but perhaps smaller. Finally, if we do not attenuate the differences between da across modalities, we expect that the effect sizes here will be comparable to previous effects.

Possibility 2:
If we do equate, or even attenuate, differences in modality for da, the patterns found in previous studies may disappear, indicating that the previous effects may have been due to overall different levels of performance. We do not list separate hypotheses for Possibility 2. 

HYPOTHESES FOR POSSIBILITY 1

Recollection:
•	We expect main effects of modality and attention, and an interaction between them.
o	Auditory recollection will be worse than visual recollection.
o	Divided attention will reduce recollection compared to full attention.
o	Divided attention will have a greater effect on visual than on auditory recollection.

Familiarity:
•	We expect an interaction and a main effect of attention but not of modality, replicating previous studies.
o	Familiarity will be better in the full attention than divided attention.
o	There will be minimal differences between audio and visual familiarity in the full attention condition. 
o	Visual familiarity will be more adversely impacted by the divided attention manipulation than auditory familiarity. 

Familiarity vs Recollection:
•	The effect size of the modality by attention interaction is expected to be smaller for familiarity than the effect size for the recollection interaction.  

da:
•	Observed da (overall recognition, not estimated from the model): We expect a main effect of attention and an interaction between modality and attention. 
o	If the attempt to increase performance in the auditory condition is successful, then da will be approximately the same for auditory 2x and visual 1x in the full attention condition
o	da will be lower under divided attention than in full attention
o	Visual da will be more adversely affected by the attention manipulation than auditory da. 

Correlations:
•	Correlations between modalities for each memory process (e.g., the correlation between recollection of auditory and of visual objects) will be examined. Based on the previous experiments, a significant correlation is expected for familiarity estimates and observed da, and a smaller relationship, potentially not significant, is expected for recollection estimates. 

Divided Attention Task:
•	The accuracy of the auditory and visual divided attention tasks is expected to be the same, whereas the RTs are expected to be greater when the task is auditory.

table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
This will be a mixed design. The order of the tests will be counterbalanced: visual first or auditory first.

Independent variables: 
attention (2 between-subjects groups) 
modality (auditory 2x, visual 1x, within subjects)

Dependent memory variables: 
process estimates of recollection
process estimates of familiarity (d’)
overall recognition da

Dependent attention variables: 
accuracy on the divided attention task 
reaction time
table.randomization:
At the level of items presented as stimuli, they will be newly randomized for each subject (randomly assigned to old or new status).
Participants will be randomly assigned to experimental conditions.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures:
We will be recruiting subjects from psychology classes at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. Students are required to earn research credit for their classes (or to write brief papers as an alternative to research participation) or are offered extra credit for their participation in research. Thus, subjects are compensated with research credits toward their classes. Some students also volunteer to take part in research without compensation. Students sign up for studies on a computerized system (SONA) that provides a brief description of each study available.
To be eligible, students must be: between the ages of 18 and 40, have no diagnosed memory impairments, no hearing impairments, be sober, and be fluent in English.
We will test subjects until we have reached a usable sample of 52, with 26 in each attention group (usable meaning that they did not have to be excluded based on eligibility criteria or performance criteria)
table.sample_size: Our sample size is n = 52 human subjects.
table.sample_size_rationale: A power analysis using G*Power 3.1 indicated that we need 50 participants in order to achieve 80% power to detect an interaction with an effect size of partial eta squared = .04. We’re rounding up to 52 in order to accommodate our counterbalance conditions. We chose a moderate effect size because it’s unclear whether the effect sizes in the previous studies would apply to repeating items or not.
table.manipulated_variables:
Modality (visual 1x or auditory 2x)
Attention (divided attention, full attention)
table.measured_variables: Measured variables include: confidence ratings in old/new judgments that will be submitted to the DPSD model to obtain estimates of recollection and familiarity. Recollection and familiarity will be analyzed; confidence ratings will not be directly analyzed. Confidence ratings will also be used to measure overall recognition (collapsed across recollection and familiarity) as indicated by da. Accuracy and reaction time will be measured for the divided attention tasks.
table.statistical_tests:
The primary research question is whether equating da across modalities will affect the interaction and main effect patterns for recollection and familiarity found in previous experiments.
Bayesian ANOVAs will be used to assess evidence for main effects and interactions between the variables. Effect sizes will also be obtained to compare between different analyses of variables that cannot be directly compared. Interactions will be followed up by Bayesian simple main effects and t-tests. Bayesian Pearson correlations will examine the relationship between memory estimates across modalities (e.g., auditory recollection and visual recollection). 

RECOLLECTION (probability estimate from the DPSD model)
We expect main effects of modality (better visual recollection) and attention (better recollection in the full attention condition), and an interaction between modality and attention, with greater effects of attention on visual than on auditory recollection. Looking specifically at the full attention condition, as a replication of three previous studies, we expect that recollection will be worse for auditory objects than for visual objects, and that this effect will be bigger than that found for familiarity.

FAMILIARITY (d’ estimate from the DPSD model)
Attention should negatively affect the familiarity estimates with greater familiarity in the full attention condition, and modality should have a small, if any, effect on familiarity. Previous studies within this paradigm have differed with respect to the interaction, and thus we leave that as an open question. Looking specifically at the full attention condition, as a replication of three previous studies, we expect that familiarity will be worse for auditory objects than for visual objects, but that the effect size will be much smaller than that found for recollection.

OVSERVED da (overall recognition, not estimated from the model)
We expect a main effect of attention, but, critically, if the change to the auditory condition (from previous studies) is successful, we should find no evidence of a difference between auditory and visual da in the full attention condition. This should result in an interaction if attention affects visual and auditory recognition differently.

Correlations between modalities for each memory process (e.g., the correlation between recollection of auditory and of visual objects) will be examined. Based on previous experiments, a significant correlation is expected for familiarity estimates and observed da, but a smaller and possibly nonsignificant correlation between the recollection estimates.

For the divided attention task, we expect no modality effect on accuracy. For RTs, we expect greater RTs in the auditory task than in the visual task.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .229", Sentence = "(two-tailed z = -2.22, p = .026), whereas the two familiarity correlations were not (two-tailed z = -1.20, p = .229)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 53 columns across 5 data files.
#### Issues Identified
1 file/column combination has at least one issue.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = "Experiment_2.xlsx", Column = "Sheet1", Issues = "⬜ Empty or unnamed columns — 1 column is empty or has a blank header"), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Spreadsheet Formatting
We examined 5 spreadsheet files in the repository; 1 has at least one formatting issue.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "Experiment_2.xlsx", Sheet = "Sheet1", 
    Issue = "Empty or unnamed columns", Detail = "1 column is empty or has a blank header."), row.names = c(NA,

metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE)
```

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 5 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Participants were 30 University of Nevada, Las Vegas (UNLV) students (M age = 21.0, 22 women) recruited from the Psychology Department's subject pool who participated in return for course credit.
Participants were instructed to memorize each item as best they could for a later memory test, and they were told that trying to identify (or label) each item would help them to remember it.

Instructions for the recognition test followed each study task; participants were asked to use a 6-point response scale to make old/new decisions about each item, with 1 anchored as "Sure New" and 6 anchored as "Sure Old".
Participants were strongly encouraged to use the whole scale across the course of each test.

At test, sounds were played for the full 2s before participants were able to respond and pictures were displayed for the full 700ms before they could respond, matching the duration times during the study phase.
Sixty participants (Mage = 18.8, 41 women, 19 men) from the UNLV Psychology Department's subject pool took part in this experiment in return for course credit.

The task was a 2-back task, presented in the modality opposite of the stimuli being encoded; thus, the n-back task was presented in black font in the middle of the computer screen when participants were studying auditory items, and was presented over headphones when studying the visual objects.
Between the presentation of each target stimulus, a number was presented and participants had to decide whether it was the same as two numbers back or not.
Participants had three seconds to respond on n-back trials (via keyboard presses) in both the auditory and visual study phases, and they practiced the task before starting the first study phase.
Participants were told it was very important to perform well on the n-back task, and that they should also memorize the objects for a later memory test.
Participants were randomly assigned to either the full or divided attention condition, and modality remained a within-subjects variable.
Seventy-eight participants (M age = 19.4, 52 women, 26 men) from the UNLV Psychology Department's subject pool took part in this experiment in return for course credit.

Several additional participants completed the experiment, but their data were excluded from analyses (using preregistered criteria): three for not using enough of the confidence scale to form an ROC, five for not doing the DA task, three for failing to use the response scale correctly, and five for low performance (d a < .20).
Sixty-four participants (M age = 20.0, 49 women) from the UNLV Psychology Department's subject pool participated in this experiment in return for course credit.

Five additional participants took part in the study but their data were excluded from analyses because they failed to understand how to use the response scale (n = 2), had poor performance (d a < .20, n = 2), or did not complete the divided attention task (n = 1).

#### File paths

**5 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `C:/Users/parksc7/Dropbox/Work/Research/Auditory Recog/Manuscript 1/1 OSF Files/Collapsed_data.xlsx` to `../1  Data/Collapsed_data.xlsx` (in Collapsed_data.Rmd); `C:/Users/parksc7/Dropbox/Work/Research/Auditory Recog/Manuscript 1/1 OSF Files/Experiment_2.xlsx` to `../1  Data/Experiment_2.xlsx` (in Experiment_2_R_markdown.Rmd); `C:/Users/parksc7/Dropbox/Work/Research/Auditory Recog/Manuscript 1/1 OSF Files/Experiment_4.xlsx` to `../1  Data/Experiment_4.xlsx` (in Experiment_4_R_markdown.Rmd); `C:/Users/parksc7/Dropbox/Work/Research/Auditory Recog/Manuscript 1/1 OSF Files/Experiment_3.xlsx` to `../1  Data/Experiment_3.xlsx` (in Experiment_3_R_markdown.Rmd); `C:/Users/parksc7/Dropbox/Work/Research/Auditory Recog/Manuscript 1/1 OSF Files/Experiment_1.xlsx` to `../1  Data/Experiment_1.xlsx` (in Experiment_1_R_markdown.Rmd). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 10 scripts: 9 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **4 scripts use an object or function that only another script defines**, so in the second run that script was loaded first, in the same session: `Experiment_1_R_markdown.R` after `Experiment_1_R_markdown.Rmd`; `Experiment_2_R_markdown.R` after `Experiment_2_R_markdown.Rmd`; `Experiment_3_R_markdown.R` after `Experiment_3_R_markdown.Rmd`; `Experiment_4_R_markdown.R` after `Experiment_4_R_markdown.Rmd`. Such a script should `source()` the other itself, since it does not run on its own. 

*a script hit an `object '...' not found` error, indicating it expected a variable another script defines. **Undefined-variable errors**

**1 script failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

**Calls that install packages in the code**

15 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.
**`library()` calls added**

**1 script uses functions from packages it does not load itself.** The packages are usually loaded in another script of the project, which only helps when the scripts run in one R session in the right order. text.text: Recognition memory on standard old/new tests is typically better for pictures than for sounds.

To investigate this modality effect, we examined the contributions of recollection and familiarity processes to recognition memory of auditory and visual objects (environmental sounds and colored line drawings, respectively).
To gain some insight into the source of the modality difference, we investigated whether the modality effect was larger for one process than the other.
Indeed, in Experiment 1, recollection was greater for visual than auditory objects, but the modality effect on familiarity was much smaller.
We replicated this pattern in all subsequent experiments.
Focusing on recollection, we examined the consequences of hindering encoding during study with a divided attention task.

Surprisingly, Experiments 2 -4 showed that divided attention at study substantially reduced visual recollection but had little effect on auditory recollection, to the point that visual recollection in the divided attention condition was similar to auditory recollection in the full attention condition.
This unusually small effect of divided attention on auditory recollection aligns with prior research showing fundamental differences in recognition of sounds and pictures.
Further, it suggests that effects we have taken as regularities in recognition (such as divided attention) may not apply to all modalities.
Confucius has been quoted as saying "I hear, and I forget.
I see, and I remember.''
Auditory memory has thus been recognized as inferior to visual memory for centuries before the claim was tested experimentally.

This phenomenon is now well established and may reflect sounds' lesser role in our lives, but they are nonetheless important, and it is not known why memory of auditory objects is worse than memory of visual objects.
We know little about episodic recognition of sounds.

There is a small amount of research examining differences between long-term recognition memory of visual and auditory objects (e.g., a picture of an object such as a bear and the sound of an object such as a car horn) and even less with respect to using memory theories to understand those differences.
With respect to memory theories, it has been tacitly assumed that what is true of visual and verbal memory should be true of auditory memory as well.

This appears to be true for printed and spoken words (e.g., Parks & Werner, 2020) but is not necessarily the case for pictures of objects and environmental sounds (e.g., Cohen et al., 2009; see Griffiths & Warren, 2004 for thoughts on auditory objects, and Chow et al., 2023, for evidence of a domain-general object recognition ability).
text.formatted: This appears to be true for printed and spoken words (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Parks & Werner, 2020)</ref> but is not necessarily the case for pictures of objects and environmental sounds (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cohen et al., 2009</ref>; see <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Griffiths & Warren, 2004</ref> for thoughts on auditory objects, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Chow et al., 2023</ref>, for evidence of a domain-general object recognition ability).

text.text: Recognition memory of visual objects is, by all accounts, extraordinary. Shepard (1967) was perhaps the first to show this, with participants recognizing 96% of 612 pictures on an immediate test, 99.7% after a two-hour delay, 92% after three days, 87% after seven days, and 57% after 120 days. Standing et al. (1970) found that under some conditions, participants could remember approximately 2,000 of an original 2,560. Standing (1973) later presented 10,000 pictures to participants, who recognized approximately 90% of them at test (Experiment 2).

(1970)</ref> found that under some conditions, participants could remember approximately 2,000 of an original 2,560. <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Standing (1973)</ref> later presented 10,000 pictures to participants, who recognized approximately 90% of them at test (Experiment 2).

text.text: Standing concluded that "the capacity for recognition memory of pictures is almost limitless" (p. 207; see also Brady et al., 2008; but see Cunningham et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Standing concluded that "the capacity for recognition memory of pictures is almost limitless" (p. 207; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Brady et al., 2008</ref>; but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Cunningham et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The same cannot be said of episodic recognition of auditory objects (or words, as seen in the picture superiority effect).

For example, Cohen et al. (2009) directly compared auditory and visual objects and found that while auditory recognition was good (d' = 1.68 and 1.83 in two experiments), it was far inferior to visual recognition (d' = 3.57).
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cohen et al. (2009)</ref> directly compared auditory and visual objects and found that while auditory recognition was good (d' = 1.68 and 1.83 in two experiments), it was far inferior to visual recognition (d' = 3.57).

text.text: Although the ease of labeling sounds had been shown to affect recognition memory (Clark et al., 1974), Cohen et al. saw no improvement when environmental sounds were labeled.
text.formatted: Although the ease of labeling sounds had been shown to affect recognition memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Clark et al., 1974)</ref>, <ref type="bibr">Cohen et al. saw</ref> no improvement when environmental sounds were labeled.

text.text: In fact, equating memory across the modalities required degrading the visual stimuli to the point of being nearly unrecognizable, demonstrating the power of visual recognition and the relative deficiency of auditory recognition.
This relative deficit was similar in musicians and nonmusicians (Cohen et al., 2011), and it was not improved by auditory training (Gloede et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This relative deficit was similar in musicians and nonmusicians <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Cohen et al., 2011)</ref>, and it was not improved by auditory training <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Gloede et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: One common criticism of studies on the modality effect is that auditory stimuli unfold over time, and the majority of the research uses static images. Bigelow and Poremba (2014) controlled for this confound by using only temporally-dynamic stimuli, and found auditory recognition was still poorer than both visual and tactile recognition.
text.formatted: One common criticism of studies on the modality effect is that auditory stimuli unfold over time, and the majority of the research uses static images. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bigelow and Poremba (2014)</ref> controlled for this confound by using only temporally-dynamic stimuli, and found auditory recognition was still poorer than both visual and tactile recognition.

text.text: However, this relative deficit is not constant across all test formats and stimulus modalities.

For example, environmental sounds are remembered as well or better than their verbal labels in free recall, but the sound deficit reappears with serial free recall (Paivio, 1975; Philipchalk & Rowe, 1971; Warren, 1969; see also Visscher et al., 2007).
text.formatted: For example, environmental sounds are remembered as well or better than their verbal labels in free recall, but the sound deficit reappears with serial free recall <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Paivio, 1975;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Philipchalk & Rowe, 1971;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Warren, 1969</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Visscher et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Although this pattern has been replicated multiple times, it has also been shown that cued recall of visual information is better than auditory when more complex and ecologically-valid materials are used (Huss & Weaver, 1996).
text.formatted: Although this pattern has been replicated multiple times, it has also been shown that cued recall of visual information is better than auditory when more complex and ecologically-valid materials are used <ref type="bibr">(Huss & Weaver, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: So, although environmental sounds can be remembered better than other materials, this appears to be restricted to a free recall of sounds vs. their labels to date, and that pattern can be explained by differences in elaborative encoding of the two stimulus types (Paivio et al., 1975).
text.formatted: So, although environmental sounds can be remembered better than other materials, this appears to be restricted to a free recall of sounds vs. their labels to date, and that pattern can be explained by differences in elaborative encoding of the two stimulus types <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Paivio et al., 1975)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, there appears to be some fundamental differences between these modalities in long-term memory, which are perhaps most consistently found when comparing sounds and pictures in recognition (Cohen et al., 2009 (Cohen et al., , 2011;; Gloede et al., 2017; Gloede & Gregg, 2019; for a review see Snyder & Gregg, 2011).
text.formatted: Thus, there appears to be some fundamental differences between these modalities in long-term memory, which are perhaps most consistently found when comparing sounds and pictures in recognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cohen et al., 2009</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Cohen et al., , 2011;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Gloede et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Gloede & Gregg, 2019</ref>; for a review see <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Snyder & Gregg, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: However, we have a limited understanding of the specific ways in which they differ.
It could be that auditory objects are inherently less memorable (e.g., Cohen et al., 2009) or that memory capacity is simply lower for environmental sounds (Snyder & Gregg, 2011).
text.formatted: It could be that auditory objects are inherently less memorable (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cohen et al., 2009)</ref> or that memory capacity is simply lower for environmental sounds <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Snyder & Gregg, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: However, these accounts seem to describe the results rather than explain them.
They also do not seem to fit with findings of similar shortterm memory abilities in the two modalities (e.g., Hawkins et al., 2025; Visscher et al., 2007; for a review see Snyder & Gregg, 2011).
text.formatted: They also do not seem to fit with findings of similar shortterm memory abilities in the two modalities (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hawkins et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Visscher et al., 2007</ref>; for a review see <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Snyder & Gregg, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: It is possible that explanations of the picture superiority effect (PSE) can also explain the visualauditory difference.
Distinctiveness of the stimuli is at least part of the cause of the PSE, given that it can be eliminated when words are made as distinctive as the pictures (Ensor et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Distinctiveness of the stimuli is at least part of the cause of the PSE, given that it can be eliminated when words are made as distinctive as the pictures <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Ensor et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This is appealing as an explanation of the audio-visual difference, but investigations to date have failed to support it (e.g., Ahmad et al., 2024), and it does not account for similarities in short-term memory performance (Snyder & Gregg, 2011).
text.formatted: This is appealing as an explanation of the audio-visual difference, but investigations to date have failed to support it (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Ahmad et al., 2024)</ref>, and it does not account for similarities in short-term memory performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Snyder & Gregg, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Other candidates for explanations have recently been investigated, including differences in the precision of representations (Gloede et al., 2017; Gloede & Gregg, 2019) and the role of gist and verbatim information (Ahmad et al., 2024). Gloede and Gregg (2019) found that the participants' percent-correct scores were better for rejecting similar lures of visual than auditory objects on an immediate recognition test, suggesting differences in the type and/or specificity of detail encoded and/or retrieved. Ahmad et al. (2024) also investigated modality differences in recognition memory with a similar-lures paradigm, and found that both verbatim and gist memory were better for pictures than sounds.

(2024)</ref> also investigated modality differences in recognition memory with a similar-lures paradigm, and found that both verbatim and gist memory were better for pictures than sounds.

text.text: In contrast, Zhang et al. (2026) argued that auditory recognition is more gist-based than visual recognition, based on fMRI evidence that auditory recognition is correlated with more "internally transformed" representations.

text.text: Overall, these findings point to the idea that visual memory may retain more fine detail than does auditory memory.
One thing missing from this line of research is the application of a theoretically-driven measurement model.

Here, we take a dual process (Jacoby, 199; Mandler, 1980) approach to measuring recognition, using the Dual Process Signal Detection (DPSD) model (Yonelinas, 1994; Yonelinas, 2002) to obtain independent estimates of recollection (the retrieval of contextual detail) and familiarity (a decontextualized feeling of prior exposure).
text.formatted: Here, we take a dual process <ref type="bibr">(Jacoby, 199;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Mandler, 1980)</ref> approach to measuring recognition, using the Dual Process Signal Detection (DPSD) model <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Yonelinas, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Yonelinas, 2002)</ref> to obtain independent estimates of recollection (the retrieval of contextual detail) and familiarity (a decontextualized feeling of prior exposure).

text.text: Until 1991, these processes were difficult to measure in accord with dual-process assumptions (e.g., that recollection and familiarity are independent).

Although the remember-know paradigm was introduced by Tulving in 1985, it assumes mutual exclusivity of recollection and familiarity (unless the estimates are corrected, Yonelinas & Jacoby, 1995). Jacoby's (1991) measurement model, the process dissociation procedure, provided a way to estimate recollection and familiarity independently.
text.formatted: Although the remember-know paradigm was introduced by Tulving in 1985, it assumes mutual exclusivity of recollection and familiarity (unless the estimates are corrected, <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Yonelinas & Jacoby, 1995)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Jacoby's (1991)</ref> measurement model, the process dissociation procedure, provided a way to estimate recollection and familiarity independently.

text.text: This was a watershed moment that generated a great deal of research, resulting in a wealth of knowledge about various aspects of cognitive control and automaticity.

For example, the debates about the model's assumptions, such as independence (e.g., Curran & Hintzman, 1995; Jacoby, 1998), proved fruitful for aging research (showing declines in recollection, but not familiarity, Jennings & Jacoby, 1993), as well as understanding other standard manipulations of memory (e.g., generate-read, Jacoby, 1991; Jennings & Jacoby, 1993; divided attention, Jacoby & Kelly, 1991; Yonelinas, 2001; levels of processing, Yonelinas, 2001).

text.text: Following Jacoby's example, in this paper we first examine whether recollection and familiarity differ for visual and auditory objects and then use an attention manipulation to undermine recollection specifically.
Our goal was to use the dual-process theory to look under the hood of the audio-visual modality effect on recognition memory to see whether (and how) it affects recollection and familiarity.

We approached the first experiment in an exploratory way, simply asking how the recognition difference for sounds and pictures is reflected in estimates of recollection and familiarity, which might suggest that one of these memory processes plays a larger role in explaining the modality difference.

Specifically, if the modality effect is larger in recollection than familiarity, it would suggest that encoding and/or retrieval of contextual detail is particularly important for understanding the modality effect.
Some evidence already points in that direction (e.g., Ahmad et al., 2024; Gloede & Gregg, 2019), but those studies did not measure recollection and familiarityfoot_0 .
text.formatted: Some evidence already points in that direction (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Ahmad et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Gloede & Gregg, 2019)</ref>, but those studies did not measure recollection and familiarity<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> .

text.text: On the other hand, if modality has no effect on the encoding and/or retrieval of contextual information, then the difference might be found primarily in familiarity.
We tested these hypotheses in the first experiment by simply manipulating modality within participants in a study-test block for each modality (counterbalanced for order).
We expected that if modality had a larger effect on one process or the other, it would be larger for recollection.

text.text: Study and test trials were blocked by modality (all of one modality at a time), and block order was counterbalanced across participants.
Study lists consisted of 80 items each, and two buffer items preceded and ended the study lists.
All study items were presented at test, as well as 80 new items.
Items were randomly assigned to old/new status for each subject.
We used E-Prime 2.0 to program the experiments.
After providing informed consent, participants read instructions for the first study task, which were reiterated by the experimenter.
Participants were instructed to memorize each item as best they could for a later memory test, and they were told that trying to identify (or label) each item would help them to remember it.
Auditory objects were presented for 2-s each, with a 2.5-s interstimulus interval (ISI).
The computer screen was blank during the auditory encoding task.
Visual objects were presented at a rate of 700 ms, with a 1-s ISI.
The visual items were presented at a faster rate than the auditory items to avoid ceiling effects.
The auditory encoding phase took 12 min and the visual study phase took 4.5 min.

Instructions for the recognition test followed each study task; participants were asked to use a 6-point response scale to make old/new decisions about each item, with 1 anchored as "Sure New" and 6 anchored as "Sure Old".
Participants were strongly encouraged to use the whole scale across the course of each test.

At test, sounds were played for the full 2s before participants were able to respond and pictures were displayed for the full 700ms before they could respond, matching the duration times during the study phase.
Once the stimulus was presented, it was removed from the screen or silenced, but the confidence scale remained onscreen and participants responded at their own pace.
Modality was manipulated within participants, and study-test block order was counterbalanced across participants.

text.text: Our goal was to compare the size of the modality effect on recollection and familiarity.
Because recollection and familiarity are on different scales, they cannot be directly compared to one another (recollection is a probability and familiarity is d', which is unbounded).

Therefore, we conducted analyses (Bayesian ANOVAs and t-tests) separately for the two parameters and compared effect sizes and Bayes factors (BF) to infer whether the manipulations affected one process more than the other (effect sizes included ƞ p 2 for ANOVA and Cohen's d for t-tests and their 95% confidence intervals) 4 .

text.text: Paired t-tests showed that there was a large difference in overall recognition (d a ) between auditory and visual modalities (BF10 = 2250.25, Cohen's d = .99, 95% CI [.54, 1.43]), replicating the typical finding of visual memory superiority.

More importantly, recollection was better in the visual than the auditory condition (BF10 = 284.17, Cohen's d = 1.06, 95% CI [0.48, 1.64]), and though this was also true for familiarity, both the effect size and the evidence were weaker (BF10 = 1.89, Cohen's d = .53, 95% CI [0.04, 1.01]).
Thus, the modality effect on recollection was larger than on familiarity, as we suspected it might be.
Note that the time it took to complete the study phase differed between the conditions, but we chose to continue with this design as a means of keeping visual recognition below ceiling.

Experiment 1 replicated the common finding that recognition is better for pictures than for sounds, and that the same pattern can be seen in both recollection and familiarity estimates.

However, modality had a bigger effect on recollection than familiarity, which indicates that participants have less access to qualitative detail about environmental sounds than pictures, which could be due to encoding and/or retrieval factors.

These results align with previous findings that discriminating between old, new, and similar-lure items is easier in the visual than the auditory modality (Gloede et al., 2017), which also points to more difficulty in accessing detailed representations.

text.text: Thus, we focused next on recollection, by undermining the ability to encode (and/or retrieve) qualitative detail.
To do this, we interleaved an nback task with the stimuli during the study phases to divide attention.

We expected that divided attention would reduce recollection in both modalities and have smaller effects on familiarity, with the open question being whether dividing attention has a different effect in the two modalities.
Sixty participants (Mage = 18.8, 41 women, 19 men) from the UNLV Psychology Department's subject pool took part in this experiment in return for course credit.

An additional five participants' data were excluded from analyses for not using enough of the scale to form an ROC (n = 1), for not making any misses in the visual condition (n = 2), for a computer crash (n = 1), and for only using "6" responses to visual items (n = 1).
Because credible evidence of differences was found in Experiment 1 with 30 participants, we used that sample size for this experiment as well, with 30 participants per full and divided conditions.
The materials were the same as those used in Experiment 1, with the addition of an n-back task with numbers between 1 and 9.

The task was a 2-back task, presented in the modality opposite of the stimuli being encoded; thus, the n-back task was presented in black font in the middle of the computer screen when participants were studying auditory items, and was presented over headphones when studying the visual objects.
When the 2-back was auditory, the spoken number words were read in a computer-generated male voice with an American accent.
The procedure for the full attention condition was the same as in Experiment 1.
Attention was divided in a second group of participants with a 2-back task.
Between the presentation of each target stimulus, a number was presented and participants had to decide whether it was the same as two numbers back or not.
The number stimuli were presented in the modality opposite of the studied stimuli.

Thus, participants in the divided attention group were presented with an object to be remembered, followed by a number with the response options same or different for the n-back task (entered via keyboard), another object, and so on.
Participants had three seconds to respond on n-back trials (via keyboard presses) in both the auditory and visual study phases, and they practiced the task before starting the first study phase.
If the participant did not respond within 3s, the program moved on to the next to-be-remembered object.
Participants were told it was very important to perform well on the n-back task, and that they should also memorize the objects for a later memory test.
The total time of the study phases differed by attention condition and modality.
Full attention auditory took 12 min and full attention visual took 4.5 minutes.
Total study time in the divided attention conditions varied per participant due to response times to the 2-back task.
However, if they took the maximum amount of time to respond to the 2-back trials, total study time would have been 20 min for the auditory condition and 12.5 min in the visual condition.
Participants were randomly assigned to either the full or divided attention condition, and modality remained a within-subjects variable.
There was no change to the test, nor to the study or test instructions, save for the explanation of the n-back task in the divided attention condition.
All ANOVAs were 2 (modality) x 2 (attention) mixed ANOVA models, with attention as a between-subjects variable and modality as a within-subjects variable.
In addition to presenting the best fitting ANOVA model, we also report the degree to which it is better than the second-best model.

Surprisingly, two-tailed independent-samples t-tests showed a decisively large effect of divided attention on visual recollection (BF10 = 317,671.40, Cohen's d = 1.65, 95% CI [1.05, 2.25]), and substantial evidence in favor of a null effect on auditory recollection (BF10 = .29, Cohen's d = .13, 95% CI [-0.39, 0.65]).
Thus, dividing attention affected visual but not auditory recollection.

This model was 1.35 times more likely than the second-best model.
Attention had a somewhat larger effect on visual (BF10 = 1845.96, d = 1.26, 95% CI [0.69, 1.82]) than auditory familiarity (BF10 = 207.26, d = 1.07, 95% CI [0.52, 1.63]).

Unexpectedly, we found that dividing attention had no detectable effect on auditory recollection but had a large effect on visual recollection (Cohen's d = .13 and d = 1.65, respectively).

text.text: The null effect of attention on auditory recollection was surprising enough that we tested it again with a new sample, and manipulated the modality of the divided attention task to make sure that it was unimportant for the results we saw in Experiment 2.

To do this, we tested three groups: full attention, divided attention with the n-back task in the modality opposite of the study items (as in Experiment 2), and divided attention with n-back in the same modality, resulting in a 3 (attention: full, divided-same, divided-different) x 2 (modality) mixed design, with modality as the within-subjects variable and attention as the between-subjects variable.
We expected to replicate the findings of Experiment 2, and to see no differences between the two divided attention tasks.

Collapsing across the divided attention groups and comparing them to the full attention group revealed decisive evidence of a large effect of attention on visual recollection (BF10 = 2.59e+9, d = 2.01, 95% CI [1.43, 2.59]), and weak evidence of a medium effect on auditory recollection (BF10 = 2.85, d = .58, 95% CI [0.09, 1.07]).

Overall, dividing attention reduced familiarity, and more so in the visual than the auditory condition.

In sum, we replicated the results of Experiment 2: divided attention (regardless of modality of the n-back task) had little to no effect on auditory recollection, but had a large effect on visual recollection.

Thus, the effects of modality (and attention) are unlikely to be due to overall recognition performance.

The findings suggest that the difference in the ability to encode and/or retrieve detail is particularly important for modality effects.

We reasoned that if the parameter estimates in the two modalities were based on similar types of memory quality and strength, we should see positive correlations between the auditory and visual conditions for each parameter.
If, however, there was a substantial difference in the quality or strength of the memories, we expected to see small or no correlations.
We collapsed across the full-attention groups' data in the first three experiments to examine post-hoc correlations between the visual and auditory recollection, and visual and auditory familiarity.

text.text: This pattern suggests that familiarity may be based on similar types of information in the two modalities (i.e., an acontextual strength signal), but that the quality of representations retrieved via recollection differs.

If this relationship is real, then it might be the case that reducing the information available to be encoded (and/or changing the way it can be encoded), would render representations in the two modalities more similar to each other.
That is, making the visual task more difficult could change the nature of the representations such that they include fewer contextual details, perhaps similar to the auditory representations.
We did this in Experiment 4 by changing the images to greyscale and speeding their presentation during encoding in both the full and divided attention condition 6 .

Examining the correlation between auditory and visual process estimates (Figure 5B, full attention conditions only), we found very strong evidence of positive correlations between modalities for both recollection (r(30) = .58, 95% CI [.29, .77], BF10 = 71.10) and familiarity (r(30) = .59, 95% CI [.31, .7,8] BF10 = 93.69).

Although it has been clear for some time that episodic recognition is better for visual than auditory objects, there is limited theory offering explanations of how and why.

Some have suggested differences in precision or fidelity (Gloede & Gregg, 2019) and/or differences in the reliance on gist and verbatim information to explain the modality effect (Ahmad et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Some have suggested differences in precision or fidelity <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Gloede & Gregg, 2019)</ref> and/or differences in the reliance on gist and verbatim information to explain the modality effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ahmad et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Zhang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: We approached the issue by examining how recognition memory processes were affected by modality and found that the effect on recollection is larger than familiarity.

This suggests that the difference between the modalities is largely due to the ability to encode and/or retrieve detail, and that simple memory strength, as indexed by familiarity estimates, plays a more minor role (at least in standard old/new recognition tests).

Moreover, correlation analyses showed that there was there was only a weak, inconclusive relationship between auditory and visual recollection (r = .18) until overall recognition (d a ) was matched between the modalities (full attention condition, Experiment 4), in which case a positive relationship emerged.
Reducing the detail and duration of the pictures seemed to render visual recognition more similar to auditory recognition, possibly by reducing the quality of the representation.

This explanation is strengthened by the fact that the correlations between auditory and visual familiarity estimates were consistently positive and did not change (significantly) when d a was matched (i.e., as would be expected of a simple strength signal devoid of qualitative detail).
To better understand the nature of the modality difference in recollection (and following Jacoby's approach to dissociations), we divided attention during the study phases of Experiments 2 -4.

We were surprised to find that the effect size of attention on recollection was much larger for pictures than for sounds, even when data were collapsed across experiments to boost power for easier detection of a small effect.

In fact, estimates of recollection in the divided attention visual condition and the full attention auditory condition were similar in Experiment 2; and in Experiments 3 and 4, recollection of visual object under divided attention fell below auditory recollection under full attention.
Thus, when sounds were encoded in ideal conditions, auditory retrieval seemed to produce at least as much detail as visual retrieval when pictures were encoded under divided attention.
This unexpected difference in effects makes attention an appealing candidate explanation for modality differences.
One possibility, then, is that the role of attention in recognition memory of visual and auditory objects differs.
However, encoding was intentional in our experiments, so attention should have been recruited similarly in the two conditions.

Another possibility is that there are more attentional lapses during encoding of auditory objects under full attention, such that adding a secondary task has little effect because attention is already divided.

However, this idea is challenged by studies of working memory and change detection that indicate that overall performance and semantic effects in auditory and visual object processing are similar (Crutcher & Beer, 2011; Hawkins et al., 2025; Irsik et al., 2016; Vanden Bosch der Nederlanden et al., 2016; Visscher et al., 2007).
text.formatted: However, this idea is challenged by studies of working memory and change detection that indicate that overall performance and semantic effects in auditory and visual object processing are similar <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Crutcher & Beer, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hawkins et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Irsik et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Vanden Bosch der Nederlanden et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Visscher et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, attention does not provide an easy explanation of modality differences, but there could be some attention-dependent component of visual recollection that is either absent, less important, or less impervious to insult than auditory recollection.

A second candidate explanation is that visual representations and/or retrieval are, on average, more precise than auditory representations/retrieval, based on performance on similar-lure tests (Ahmad et al., 2024; Gloede & Gregg, 2019).
text.formatted: A second candidate explanation is that visual representations and/or retrieval are, on average, more precise than auditory representations/retrieval, based on performance on similar-lure tests <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ahmad et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Gloede & Gregg, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Gloede and Gregg suggested that this could be due to the speed with which visual and auditory features of a stimulus can be perceived and encoded.
Participants can sample static visual objects more than dynamic auditory objects, and connecting the stimulus to its meaning may be faster for visual than for auditory objects.
If so, there would be more time for encoding, elaboration and/or rehearsal of pictures, and the modality difference could be attributed to functional presentation and rehearsal time differences.

Importantly though, we purposefully confounded presentation and ISI time with modality: auditory objects were 2-s long and had a 2.5-s ISI, whereas visual objects (in Experiments 1 -3) appeared on screen for 700 ms, with a 1-s ISI.

This confound should ensure that modality effects are not just a function of stimulus duration, but given the fundamental timing differences between auditory and visual processing, it is difficult to rule this out entirely.
Similarly, Ensor et al. (2019) noted that visual stimuli may have an encoding advantage because their features appear simultaneously whereas auditory features necessarily unfold over time.
text.formatted: Similarly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Ensor et al. (2019)</ref> noted that visual stimuli may have an encoding advantage because their features appear simultaneously whereas auditory features necessarily unfold over time.

text.text: As such, the ability to bind features together may be more difficult for sounds than pictures (but see Bigelow & Poremba, 2014), resulting in poorer access to fine detail at test.
text.formatted: As such, the ability to bind features together may be more difficult for sounds than pictures (but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bigelow & Poremba, 2014)</ref>, resulting in poorer access to fine detail at test.

text.text: Although one might expect that auditory recollection would then be at floor in a divided attention condition, the effects of attention on memory precision have not yet been established in long-term memory to our knowledge.
Another possibility is that auditory and visual objects may differ in their degrees of conceptual and perceptual distinctiveness (feature overlap).
Konkle et al. (2010 items was based on participants' subjective judgments.

text.text: So, it could also be the case that there actually is greater feature overlap among the auditory objects, rendering them less discriminable, even if participants did not detect it, although that seems unlikely.
Our stimuli differed from theirs though, so we cannot rule out the possibility that distinctiveness was greater for our visual than auditory stimuli.
It will be useful to examine whether controlling distinctiveness eliminates the modality effect.
In general, studies of auditory and visual recognition memory have not done much to match the stimuli on various features that we typically would for words, such as frequency or nameability.

Additionally, memory of verbs is often more sensitive to context than memory for nouns (e.g., Earles & Kersten, 2017; Kersten & Earles, 2004; Reynolds & Flagg, 1976); that is, sounds are more likely to reflect verbs (e.g., barking) because static objects tend not to make sound, whereas pictures are more likely to depict static objects and therefore reflect nouns (e.g., a vase).

text.text: A comparison of pictures reflecting verbs (e.g., an image of a dog barking) and sounds will be important.
Additionally, the total time of the encoding phases differed across modalities.
Although this was necessary to keep visual performance below ceiling, an experiment that holds study time equal across conditions will be needed.
In sum, there are still a number of methodological factors to rule out as potential causes of the auditory-visual modality effect.
The finding that divided attention had little effect on auditory recollection but a substantial effect on visual recollection raises questions about how recollection works in general.
A tacit assumption of memory theories is that the processes they propose should work similarly across domains, and yet the data presented here suggest that that may not always be the case.
Memory models have been routinely built on data from experiments on verbal and visual stimuli, but our findings suggest that we need to include other stimuli too.

For instance, is it the case that there is something unique about auditory stimuli that reduces recollection (e.g., different levels of encoded and/or retrieved detail available), and/or could it be that recollection operates somewhat differently in different modalities?

For example, Parks et al. (2011) found that recollection in source memory tasks operated differently depending on the complexity of the stimuli; recollection of more complex stimuli showed more variance than recollection of simple stimuli.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Parks et al. (2011)</ref> found that recollection in source memory tasks operated differently depending on the complexity of the stimuli; recollection of more complex stimuli showed more variance than recollection of simple stimuli.

text.text: This suggests that we should investigate other traditional manipulations (e.g., repetition, spacing, etc.) to see if they affect memory processes similarly (in the same direction and/or to the same extent) for the two modalities.
