Familiarity suffered under divided attention (main effect attention in collapsed data (F(1, 166) = 86.02, ƞ p2 = .34, 95% CI [0.23, 0.44]) to about the same extent as recollection did (main effect attention in collapsed data (F(1, 166) = 85.32, ƞ p2 = .34, 95% CI [0.23, 0.44];
Fs are presented here because the values are the same at two decimal places).
This was not the focus of our experiments and thus we hesitate to interpret it, but it is worth noting that dividing attention with an n-back task might be a fairly extreme manipulation of attention.
Most studies on divided attention and memory have used somewhat easier secondary tasks (e.g., detecting three odd digits in a row).

Research on dual-task performance has shown that it is the combination of task demands that determines the extent of performance impairments (e.g., Hirst & Kalamar, 1987), and those effects are greatest when the two tasks rely on the same or highly-overlapping processes.
text.formatted: Research on dual-task performance has shown that it is the combination of task demands that determines the extent of performance impairments (e.g., Hirst & Kalamar, 1987), and those effects are greatest when the two tasks rely on the same or highly-overlapping processes.

text.text: Combining two memory tasks might produce one of the largest divided attention effects on recognition because they depend so heavily on similar processes and resources.
Thus, it seems logical that different ways of dividing attention could produce different effects on recognition memory.
It will be important to see if our current results replicate when other secondary tasks are used, or when recollection is undermined in other ways.
Furthermore, testing a wide range of divided attention tasks to determine whether different secondary tasks have different consequences for memory processes may be warranted.
For example, we do not know whether an n-back task would substantially reduce familiarity for words.
A major limitation of studying differences between visual and auditory recognition memory is that they have different temporal characteristics.
Auditory objects are inherently dynamic, whereas the visual stimuli we used were stationary and rather simple (colored line drawings).
However, some evidence suggests that auditory memory is still inferior to visual memory even when temporal dynamics are controlled and equated in the two modalities (Bigelow & Poremba, 2014).
text.formatted: However, some evidence suggests that auditory memory is still inferior to visual memory even when temporal dynamics are controlled and equated in the two modalities <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bigelow & Poremba, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Nonetheless, it would be ideal to compare sounds to silent videos to better equate the stimuli on the temporal dimension.
Similarly, we equated overall recognition in Experiment 4 by reducing recognition of pictures, but it will be important to do it by improving auditory recognition as well.
We have focused on recollection because the modality effect was larger and because of the unexpected effects of dividing attention in the two modalities.
However, familiarity differed substantially as well.

Images presented for 700 ms produced a stronger familiarity signal than sounds presented for 2 s under full attention in Experiments 1 -3 (collapsed data: BF10 = 163.82, d = .48, 95% CI [0.23, 0.72]).
This simple strength difference is interesting in its own right.
Future work controlling stimulus features, using different ways of equating overall recognition, and timing are likely needed.
Overall, we showed that the effect of audio-visual modality was much larger on recollection than on familiarity in an old/new item recognition test.
Surprisingly, we also found that dividing attention affected auditory and visual recollection differently, which raises a number of questions about recollection and the variables that affect it.
The next task is to delve into the nature of those differences.
For example, one question that needs to be answered is whether auditory recognition is worse due to encoding, retrieval, or both.

Investigating these questions, the candidate explanations for differences, as well as the neural underpinnings of auditory object memory (e.g., MTL -auditory cortex connections, Billig et al., 2022) will hold some clues about the nature of the difference between memory for visual and auditory objects.
text.formatted: Investigating these questions, the candidate explanations for differences, as well as the neural underpinnings of auditory object memory (e.g., MTL -auditory cortex connections, <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Billig et al., 2022)</ref> will hold some clues about the nature of the difference between memory for visual and auditory objects.

text.text: Further examination of the relationship between recognition memory and conceptual and perceptual distinctiveness led the authors to conclude that conceptual distinctiveness lay at the heart of excellent recognition of images.
This might suggest that visual superiority is therefore due to conceptual information, but Konkle et al. looked only at visual stimuli.

Ahmad et al. (2024) looked at this possibility using a different way of measuring conceptual and perceptual distinctiveness and concluded that the modality difference in their study could not be attributed to one type of distinctiveness more than the other.

Thus, there is currently no evidence in the memory literature to support the idea that the visual memory advantage is caused by greater visual distinctiveness, but the questions about the roles of conceptual and perceptual information and feature overlap are still far from resolved.
